snippet.title: Why Hippos Secret a Red Fluid (And It's Not Blood) #shorts
snippet.description:
That's not blood. It's a red secretion from a hippo's skin. And it's not sweat, either. It comes from special glands deep under the skin. At first, it's colorless. Then it turns red, then brown. The red pigment works like sunscreen. The orange one fights bacteria. Together, they protect a hippo's sensitive skin from sunburn and infection. It just stains your hands.

Here's what's actually happening. The fluid is produced by subdermal glands — not sweat glands, which hippos lack entirely. It's an oily, alkaline secretion with a pH between 8.5 and 10.5 (Saikawa et al., Nature, 2004). When it first comes out, it's colorless. But within minutes of exposure to air, it polymerizes and turns red, then brown (Saikawa et al., 2004).

The chemistry is what makes it remarkable. The red pigment is called hipposudoric acid. The orange one is norhipposudoric acid. Both are non-benzenoid aromatic compounds — a rare class of molecules (Saikawa et al., Nature, 2004). Their UV-visible spectra show strong absorption between 200 and 600 nanometers. That's the range of ultraviolet light that causes sunburn. So the pigments act as a built-in sunscreen (Saikawa et al., 2004; Hashimoto et al., 2004).

But the red pigment does more than block UV. It also has antibiotic properties. At concentrations lower than those found on a hippo's skin, it inhibits the growth of Pseudomonas aeruginosa and Klebsiella pneumoniae — two bacteria that cause serious infections in humans (Saikawa et al., 2004; ABC Science, 2004). This helps explain why hippos rarely get infected, even when they have open wounds from fighting.

The secretion also serves other purposes. It moisturizes the skin, repels water, and helps control body temperature (Scientific American, 2002; Britannica). Hippos have very thin epidermis and no sebaceous glands, so their skin is extremely sensitive to drying and sunburn. This secretion is their only protection.

So the next time you see a hippo covered in red, don't assume it's injured. It's not. It's wearing its own sunscreen. And it works better than most of ours.
